message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This audit is based on the full appointment record for six months, all 24,860 booked appointments, rather than a sample, so the figures are complete and the rates are exact. We were careful with definitions, separating genuine DNAs from late cancellations, and we costed the impact in clinical time so the Division can see what is at stake: around £80,900 every six months. The most useful finding is about reminder calls. Patients who received a call had a DNA rate of 6.0% against 12.5% for those who did not, which shows that a simple, low-tech intervention the service already uses more than halves missed appointments. Extending it is the obvious, practical step, and it uses staff and processes that are already in place, so it does not need new funding. We also identified concrete, fixable weaknesses in the discharge policy and in refilling late cancellations. I believe the recommendations are proportionate and will bring the service within target.
</author>

<document>
Internal Audit Memo: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy
To: Director of Operations, Therapies Division
From: Clinical Audit Team
Date: 14 August 2026

1. Scope
This audit examined missed appointments in the outpatient physiotherapy service across our three clinic sites between 1 January and 30 June 2026. For the purposes of this audit, a "did not attend" (DNA) is recorded when a patient fails to attend without giving notice. Late cancellations (less than 24 hours' notice) are recorded and reported separately, because the slot can sometimes be offered to another patient. We reviewed the appointment system records for all 24,860 booked appointments in the period and interviewed reception and clinical staff at each site.

2. Overall position
There were 2,610 DNAs in the period, a DNA rate of 10.5%, against the service target of 8%. Each DNA leaves a 30-minute clinical slot unused. At the service's average cost per clinical hour of £62, the 1,305 lost clinical hours represent around £80,900 of clinical time over six months.

Table 1. DNA rate by appointment type
Appointment type | Booked | DNAs | DNA rate
New patient assessment | 6,210 | 410 | 6.6%
Follow-up | 18,650 | 2,200 | 11.8%
Total | 24,860 | 2,610 | 10.5%

Follow-up appointments account for most DNAs. Staff told us that many patients stop attending once their symptoms improve, without telling the service.

3. Reminder calls
Since 2024, reception staff have phoned patients two working days before their appointment where time allows. In the audit period, staff made reminder calls for 7,800 appointments, about 300 a week over the 26 weeks. A call is recorded as received only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend; unanswered calls are not recorded. Reception staff estimate that each call, including dialling, rescheduling where needed and updating the record, takes an average of four minutes.

Table 2. DNA rate by reminder status
Reminder status | Appointments | DNAs | DNA rate
Reminder call received | 7,800 | 470 | 6.0%
No reminder call recorded | 17,060 | 2,140 | 12.5%

Patients who received a reminder call were less than half as likely to miss their appointment. Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate, and extending them to all appointments would bring the service well within its 8% target.

4. Discharge policy
The service's policy is that a patient who DNAs twice without explanation is discharged back to their referrer. We found the policy was applied inconsistently: of 160 patients who met the criterion, 104 were discharged. Staff were reluctant to discharge patients they knew to be vulnerable.

5. Late cancellations
In addition to the DNAs above, 1,140 appointments were cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice. Reception staff were able to refill 31% of these slots, usually with patients on the cancellation list.

6. Findings and recommendations
Finding 1. The DNA rate of 10.5% (including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs) is above target and costs the service around £80,900 in clinical time every six months.
Recommendation 1. Extend reminder calls to all booked appointments, about 960 a week, using reception staff. This can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost.

Finding 2. The two-DNA discharge policy is applied inconsistently.
Recommendation 2. Revise the policy to include a documented clinical review before discharge, so that vulnerable patients are protected and the policy can then be applied consistently.

Finding 3. Late-cancellation slots are refilled only 31% of the time.
Recommendation 3. Introduce an automated text offer to patients on the cancellation list when a slot becomes free.

7. Conclusion
Missed appointments are costly but largely preventable. Reminder calls have been shown to more than halve DNAs in this service, and extending them to every patient, together with the policy and process changes above, should bring the DNA rate below target within six months.
</document>
response:
# Review: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy

The memo is clear and well organised, and the arithmetic in Tables 1 and 2 and the £80,900 figure all check out. But its central claim, that reminder calls more than halve DNAs, isn't supported by the data as recorded. The headline recommendation also has a staffing cost the memo says doesn't exist. These problems sit in the parts you describe as the most useful, so they need fixing before this goes to the Director.

## Major issues

### 1. The reminder-call comparison is biased and can't show cause and effect

Section 3 says a call "is recorded as received only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend; unanswered calls are not recorded." This creates two problems:

- **The "received" group is pre-selected for attendance.** It contains only patients who picked up and said they would come. Anyone who said they couldn't make it was rescheduled, so they drop out of this group.
- **The "no reminder" group includes failed calls.** Patients who were phoned but didn't answer are counted as "no reminder call recorded." Patients who are hard to reach by phone are plausibly the ones most likely to DNA.

On top of this, calls were made "where time allows," which isn't random. If calls went disproportionately to new patients (6.6% DNA rate) rather than follow-ups (11.8%), that alone would produce some of the gap. The memo doesn't break Table 2 down by appointment type, so we can't tell.

So the 6.0% vs 12.5% gap mixes any real effect of calling with the effect of *who answers and confirms*. The statement "Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate" (Section 3), and "have been shown to more than halve DNAs" (Section 7), are not supported.

Your note says the full census makes "the rates exact." That's true for sampling error: the rates are exact descriptions of these records. But a census does nothing about selection bias or how outcomes were recorded, which is the problem here.

**Suggested fixes:**
- Reword as an association. For example: "Patients who answered a reminder call and confirmed attendance had a DNA rate of 6.0%, compared with 12.5% for all other appointments. Because only answered, confirmed calls are recorded, this comparison overstates the effect of calling, and we cannot estimate the true effect from current data."
- Stratify Table 2 by appointment type if the data allow.
- Recommend recording **every call attempt and its outcome** (answered/confirmed, answered/rescheduled, no answer). Then compare all *attempted* calls against no attempt.
- Better still, recommend a short pilot, e.g. calling on alternate weeks or at alternate sites, to measure the real effect before rolling out.

### 2. The projection to "well within target" doesn't follow

Even if calling did cause the gap, extending calls to everyone wouldn't give everyone a 6.0% rate. Some patients won't answer, and the 6.0% applies only to those who did and confirmed. Without an answer rate, the memo can't project a service-wide figure. "Well within its 8% target" (Section 3) and "below target within six months" (Section 7) should be removed or heavily qualified.

### 3. "No additional cost" is contradicted by the memo's own figures

Using the memo's numbers:

| | Calls/week | Minutes/call | Hours/week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current | 300 | 4 | 20 |
| Proposed (all appointments) | ~960 | 4 | 64 |
| **Additional** | 660 | | **~44** |

An extra 44 hours a week is about 1.2 full-time staff at 37.5 hours. Two things make it worse:

- The four-minute estimate covers recorded calls. Unanswered attempts also take time but aren't counted.
- Calls are currently made only "where time allows," which suggests reception has no spare capacity now.

The claim that extra calls "can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost" (Recommendation 1), and your note's "does not need new funding," need either evidence or replacing. A cost estimate would be better: about 1,140 extra reception hours per six months, set against the expected recovery of clinical time.

**Consider an alternative:** Recommendation 3 already proposes automated texts for the cancellation list. Automated SMS reminders would cost far less per contact than phone calls, and could be paired with calls targeted at higher-risk groups (e.g. follow-ups, or patients with a previous DNA). This would make Recommendation 1 much more defensible.

### 4. Finding 1 contradicts the memo's own definitions

Section 1 states that late cancellations "are recorded and reported separately." Finding 1 says the 10.5% rate includes late cancellations, "which we classify as DNAs." Both can't be true, and the figures show the Section 1 version is correct:

- 10.5% = 2,610 / 24,860, i.e. DNAs only.
- If the 1,140 late cancellations were included, the rate would be 3,750 / 24,860 = **15.1%**.

Since your note highlights careful definitions as a strength, this inconsistency will undermine reader confidence. Delete the parenthetical in Finding 1.

## Moderate issues

- **The £80,900 is unused clinical time, not cash.** Clinicians may use DNA slots for notes or admin, so this isn't a saving the Division can bank. Describe it as "the value of clinical time not used for patient care" rather than implying recoverable money.
- **Late cancellations aren't costed.** About 787 unfilled late-cancellation slots (1,140 × 69%) represent roughly another £24,400 of clinical time, assuming 30-minute slots. Including this would strengthen the case for Recommendation 3.
- **The follow-up finding isn't followed through.** Staff report that follow-up patients stop attending once symptoms improve. That points to an option the memo doesn't mention: patient-initiated follow-up, where patients book their own follow-ups as needed. It addresses the largest source of DNAs directly and should at least be considered.
- **The discharge policy finding isn't linked to DNAs.** 104 of 160 patients (65%) were discharged as per policy. Recommendation 2 is sensible on safeguarding grounds. However, the memo doesn't say whether consistent application would reduce the DNA rate. It mainly removes patients from the list. State what outcome is expected.

## Minor points

- Section 3 says calls are made "two working days before." It's worth noting how appointments booked at shorter notice would be handled under full roll-out.
- Recommendation 3 has no cost or expected uplift on the 31% refill rate. Even a rough target would help.
- The Conclusion's "largely preventable" is stronger than the evidence supports. "Partly preventable" or "may be reducible" would be safer.

## Summary of suggested changes

1. Reframe the reminder-call result as an association, explain the recording bias, and remove the causal and target-attainment claims.
2. Recommend recording all call attempts, plus a pilot or SMS trial before full roll-out.
3. Replace "no additional cost" with an honest staffing estimate (~44 extra hours/week).
4. Remove "including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs" from Finding 1.
5. Describe £80,900 as the value of clinical time, and consider adding the late-cancellation cost.
6. Consider patient-initiated follow-up as an option for the follow-up DNA problem.

With these changes, the memo would still make a strong case for action on reminders. It would also be robust to scrutiny from the Director or finance colleagues, which the current version may not be.
